commons:8943891.summary: In a lunette of the crypt at Hosios Loukas, the body of Christ is laid out on a slab, the Virgin bending close over him while two mourners and a winged angel attend on the right. Painted for the burial crypt beneath the monastery church, the scene of Christ's burial had a special meaning in a place of tombs, where the monks awaited the resurrection he made possible.
facts: The crypt has eight lunettes with scenes of Christ's Passion and Resurrection, together with forty medallion portraits of apostles, martyrs and abbots.
The frescoes are believed to date mostly after 1048 and the death of Theodore Leobachus, a patron who became abbot.
Hidden under centuries of dust, the paintings were cleaned by the Greek Archaeological Service in the 1960s.
commons:8943891.notes: The scene could also be read as a Lamentation; the Commons category names it the Entombment.

cur:objects-berlin-raising-of-lazarus-iv.summary: Christ, followed by his apostles, strides toward the tomb and stretches out his right hand, commanding Lazarus to come forth; Lazarus stands wrapped in his grave-bands in an arched tomb while a servant unwinds them. Martha and Mary kneel at Christ's feet in gratitude. Coming just before Palm Sunday in the Byzantine calendar, the Raising of Lazarus was celebrated as a pledge of the general resurrection.
facts: In the Byzantine Church the Saturday before Palm Sunday is still called 'Lazarus Saturday', and this scene was one of the regular feast images (tradition).
Traces of gilding on the figures show that such ivories were originally enriched with colour and gold (type).

cur:objects3-sancta-sanctorum-nativity-s.summary: Inside a roundel bordered by flowers, this heavy silk shows the newborn Christ, swaddled in the manger, with the ox and the ass leaning over him; a haloed figure stands at the left and a large seated figure fills the right of the scene. The silk was used to wrap or cover one of the relics in the Sancta Sanctorum, the private chapel of the popes at the Lateran, and so survived the centuries in the dark of the papal treasury.
facts: It belongs with a companion silk of the same weave showing the Annunciation (Vatican inv. 61231); both were used in the Sancta Sanctorum and are now in the Vatican Museums.

The Sancta Sanctorum, first mentioned in the Liber Pontificalis under Pope Stephen III (768–772), served as the popes' private oratory; its main altar held a cypress-wood relic chest placed there by Pope Leo III (795–816).

links.label: Image on Wikimedia Commons (with museum label)

cur:objects3-sancta-sanctorum-nativity-s.notes: Date and possible Syrian origin follow the Vatican Museums label quoted on Commons. The identities of the haloed standing figure and the seated figure (the Virgin, Joseph or a midwife) are not given on the label and are left open here.

vam:O88287.summary: Above, Christ stands in a tall oval mandorla between Moses and Elijah on the mountain; below, Peter, James and John fall to the ground, one shielding himself and another pointing up in awe at the vision. The plaque, framed with foliage, captures the moment when the disciples glimpsed the divine glory of their Master.
facts: The plaque is a companion to the V&A's Healing of the Blind Man and the Leper (255-1867); both were probably made for a book cover in Metz about 870–880.
Both plaques were purchased from the Webb collection for £25 each (V&A).
vam:O88287.notes: The ivory is split vertically and a small piece of the top border is missing.

Q18686031.summary: The newborn Christ lies naked and tiny on the bare ground, light streaming from his body, while Mary, Joseph, angels and three wonderfully rough, awestruck shepherds kneel around him. Hugo van der Goes gives every figure a solemn individuality, and fills the foreground with a still life of flowers whose symbolism points ahead to the Passion. Its arrival in Florence astonished Italian painters and changed the way they painted the Nativity.
facts: It was commissioned by Tommaso Portinari, manager of the Medici bank in Bruges, and shipped to Florence for the church of Sant'Egidio at the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, where it arrived in 1483.
The image of the Child lying on the ground radiating light is probably based on the vision of the Nativity described by Saint Bridget of Sweden.
Its realistic shepherds directly inspired Domenico Ghirlandaio's Adoration of the Shepherds in the Sassetti Chapel (1485).
